texts.text: In July 1964, inspecting rice ear by ear in a paddy at Anjiang Agricultural School in Hunan province, the instructor Yuan Longping spotted a peculiar plant.
It was male-sterile, shedding no viable pollen.
Rice pollinates itself, so breeding hybrid seed in bulk depends on such plants.

texts.text: In February 1966 he detailed the anomaly in the journal Chinese Science Bulletin.
The specimen launched a six-year hunt: Yuan and his colleagues could not breed a sterile line whose offspring reliably inherited the trait.
The breakthrough came on 23 November 1970, in a marsh near Nanhong Farm in Sanya, Hainan.

texts.text: Yuan's assistant, Li Bihu, and Feng Keshan, a farm technician, found wild rice whose pollen was abortive.

texts.text: Then came Yuan's decisive move: rather than withhold the strain, he distributed it to collaborators nationwide.
Hybrids need three distinct lines: a sterile line, one to maintain its sterility, and one to restore fertility in the hybrids.
Yan Longan's team in Jiangxi bred sterile lines and Zhang Xiancheng in Guangxi first identified a restorer line.

islands.words: and Zhang Xiancheng in Guangxi first

texts.text: In October 1973, at a national conference in Suzhou, Yuan declared the three-line system complete.
By 1976 hybrids were under cultivation on about 140,000 hectares.
The World Food Prize Foundation estimates that hybrid rice can yield up to a fifth more grain than conventional varieties.
By the early 2000s it covered almost half of China's rice fields.
Yuan Longping, who shared the 2004 World Food Prize with Sierra Leone's Monty Jones, died in Changsha on 22 May 2021, aged 91.
Yet popular myth portrays him as a solitary genius.
His eye began the search; his generosity let many hands bring in the harvest.
